title: Hajar, unnamed and remembered
hookLine: unnamed in the Qur'an, remembered by every pilgrim who runs between the hills

cards: Every year at the Hajj, and all year round at the 'umrah, crowds walk back and forth between two low hills in Mecca, as-Safa and al-Marwah. Seven lengths.
Along part of the way, green lights mark a stretch where men break into a jog. Grandmothers in wheelchairs are pushed along it. Children ride on shoulders.
Every one of them is retracing the steps of a single mother, alone, looking for water. The Qur'an never says her name.

teach.b: The Qur'an gives the outline. In surah fourteen, Ibrahim prays: our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley with no crops, by Your sacred House.
And in al-Baqarah, as-Safa and al-Marwah are named among the signs of Allah. The woman herself is left out. Her name, Hajar, and her story come from a long hadith in al-Bukhari, told by Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibrahim brings her and the baby Isma'il to the empty valley with a bag of dates and a skin of water, and turns to go. She follows him: are you leaving us here, where there's no one and nothing? She asks again and again.
Then she asks a different question: did Allah command you to do this? He says yes. And she answers: then He will not abandon us.
She goes back. The water runs out. The baby cries.
She climbs as-Safa to look for anyone, sees no one, hurries down through the valley and up al-Marwah. Seven times. The Prophet ﷺ said, in that same hadith: that is why people go between them.
Then she hears a voice, and an angel strikes the ground, and water comes up: Zamzam. She hurries to wall it in with her hands.
The Prophet said, may Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il; if she'd left it, it would have become a flowing stream. The Bible knows her as Hagar and tells her story in its own way.
In Islam, her search became a rite. Unnamed in the book, she sets the pace for every pilgrim.

how: Pilgrims at the Hajj and 'umrah walk seven times between as-Safa and al-Marwah (the sa'y), with many men jogging between the green markers, and drink Zamzam water, remembering Hajar's search.

o: the pilgrim's walk between the two hills
Isma'il's mother, whose search became the sa'y
the spring of water that rose up in Mecca

p: the two hills, among Allah's signs

s: it doesn't; her name and story come from hadith.
pilgrims' walk between the hills follows her search for water
the Prophet said: that is why people go between them.
in the hadith an angel strikes the ground, and Hajar walls in the water with her hands.

games.q: you're Hajar. Ibrahim is walking away, leaving you and the baby in an empty valley. you've asked why, and he won't answer. what do you ask next?
o: did Allah command you to do this?
games.why: she asks if Allah commanded it. he says yes, and she says: then He will not abandon us.

practice: Let someone come to mind whose effort holds your life up and whose name almost no one knows: the person who cleans your building, a grandparent who crossed a border with nothing, a teacher you never thanked.
Picture them doing the work, back and forth, like Hajar between the hills, and say their name if you know it, or hold their face if you don't. If you pray, you can ask mercy for them.

wordCard.voice: Hajar. Mother of Isma'il, unnamed in the Qur'an, named in hadith: her seven runs between as-Safa and al-Marwah became the sa'y of every pilgrim. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Hajar, the mother of Isma'il.

carryVoice: Your line: unnamed, never forgotten. Seven runs, and every pilgrim since. That's day six hundred seventy-five.
